title: Open in medias res — begin in the middle of something happening
source_claim: Open scenes with characters already engaged in action, conflict, or a situation that gives the reader/viewer something to track immediately. Don't begin with static setup.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Consistent across fiction craft sources. Not tested for spoken video scripts specifically.
reported_exceptions: When the setting itself IS the story beat (e.g., discovering a destroyed city), description can carry the opening (S02). Educational/explainer content may need context-first openings.
direct_evidence: S01/S02 advise entering at instability/action; genre and medium transfer are unproven.
notes: S01/S02 advise entering at instability/action; genre and medium transfer are unproven.

title: First-page/first-scene hook check
source_claim: The opening scene must plant a question, establish a character worth following, or present a situation that demands resolution. Use the openings reference checklist to verify.
reported_evidence: AR (author recommendation within a structured skill)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source, but consistent with broader craft consensus.
reported_exceptions: Tutorial/explainer formats may use a problem-statement hook instead of a narrative one.
direct_evidence: First-page hook checklist appears in S01; first-page fiction heuristic is not a universal video-script law.
notes: First-page hook checklist appears in S01; first-page fiction heuristic is not a universal video-script law.

title: Narrative summary opening formula — 15–25 words establishing the content type
source_claim: When summarizing or introducing content, open with a plain descriptor in 15–25 words that tells the audience what kind of content this is (interview, paper, documentary).
reported_confidence: Low. Single source, task-specific prompt pattern.
reported_exceptions: Does not apply to immersive fiction or in-medias-res documentary openings.
direct_evidence: 15–25-word opening is present in a specific S03 story-explanation prompt, not a general script mandate.
notes: 15–25-word opening is present in a specific S03 story-explanation prompt, not a general script mandate.

title: Three-act as default, not mandate
source_claim: Three-act structure is the default when genre is unclear, but stories should use the structure that fits their form and genre. Short forms have separate reference structures. Multi-genre stories load multiple genre packs and resolve conflicts with the author.
reported_evidence: CS (cross-source — with caveat that S55 derives from Truby's published work)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Widely acknowledged in craft, but not empirically demonstrated as superior to alternatives.
reported_exceptions: Explanatory nonfiction may use question-driven or argument-driven structures instead (S24 review skill). Interactive narratives use node/graph structures (S51, S52).
direct_evidence: S01 recommends three-act only as a default when genre is unclear; framed as book/genre workflow.
notes: S01 recommends three-act only as a default when genre is unclear; framed as book/genre workflow.

title: Beats mapped to chapters with gap/clustering detection
source_claim: Plot beats should be assigned to chapters, and pacing diagnostics should warn about beats that bunch up (rushed middles) or leave long gaps (sagging middles).
reported_scope: FS (long-form narrative — novels, series, long documentaries)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Structural principle supported by craft consensus.
reported_exceptions: Short-form video doesn't operate on chapter/beat granularity.
direct_evidence: S01 explicitly maps beats to chapters; applicability to long documentary scripts is extrapolated.
notes: S01 explicitly maps beats to chapters; applicability to long documentary scripts is extrapolated.

title: Scene-sequel pattern — reaction, dilemma, decision
source_claim: After a scene's goal-conflict-outcome, include a sequel where characters (and the audience) process what happened: reaction to the outcome, facing a dilemma, then making a decision that drives the next scene.
reported_confidence: Moderate. Well-known craft model. Not empirically validated for audience response.
reported_exceptions: Action sequences may compress or skip sequels for pacing. Horror uses recovery periods as a specific application.
direct_evidence: S01 attributes framework to Dwight Swain and states not every scene needs a sequel; U classification too broad.
notes: S01 attributes framework to Dwight Swain and states not every scene needs a sequel; U classification too broad.

title: Try-fail cycles with outcome values
source_claim: Scenes should have clear outcomes coded as: yes, no, yes-but, no-and. Pacing dashboards should warn about runs of easy wins (too many "yes" outcomes), which reduce tension.
reported_scope: FS (fiction, narrative nonfiction with dramatic structure)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single primary source for the specific coding system, but try-fail is broadly acknowledged.
reported_exceptions: Expository/educational content doesn't operate on try-fail cycles.
direct_evidence: Four try/fail outcomes are source-authored craft model, not empirically universal.
notes: Four try/fail outcomes are source-authored craft model, not empirically universal.

title: Story opportunity assessment — GO / INVESTIGATE / STOP
source_claim: Before committing to a nonfiction story, assess: observable action, access to people/places, character interaction, scope feasibility, presence of change/choice, and connection to a larger issue. Decision: GO (all present), INVESTIGATE (some gaps to fill), or STOP (fundamental gap).
reported_evidence: PP (professional practice — adapted from published nonfiction methodology)
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Derived from established nonfiction methodology. Source provenance: adapted from a published Harvard nonfiction curriculum.
reported_exceptions: Fiction doesn't need access assessment. Educational content doesn't need dramatic change.
direct_evidence: S24 GO/INVESTIGATE/STOP expressly described as compilation labels; not original Harvard taxonomy.
notes: S24 GO/INVESTIGATE/STOP expressly described as compilation labels; not original Harvard taxonomy.

title: Hierarchical structure — scene/beat within arc/act within story
source_claim: Narrative content benefits from hierarchical organization: Knots (scenes/chapters) contain Stitches (beats/moments), organized within Arcs, which form the overall story. This enables modular construction and reordering.
reported_evidence: CS (three sources, though S51/S52 are for interactive narrative)
reported_scope: U (universal principle, though implementation varies by format)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Structural principle broadly supported. Interactive sources are partially transferable.
reported_exceptions: Very short content (social media, Shorts) may not need multiple hierarchy levels.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Alternate high- and low-tension beats within a scene
source_claim: Sustained intensity numbs the reader/viewer. Alternate high-tension and low-tension beats to maintain engagement. After a peak, give the audience recovery time.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Consistent across sources. Horror-specific application well-articulated.
reported_exceptions: Action sequences may deliberately sustain intensity for short bursts. Educational content may have different tension rhythms.
direct_evidence: S02 specifically recommends alternating high/lower-tension beats; no demonstrated viewer-retention effect.
notes: S02 specifically recommends alternating high/lower-tension beats; no demonstrated viewer-retention effect.

title: End chapters/sections on forward momentum
source_claim: End narrative segments on an open question, a new complication, or an emotional shift — something that makes the audience want to continue.
reported_scope: U (all narrative formats; YouTube retention, podcast episodes, series installments)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Consistent craft advice. Not measured against audience retention data in these sources.
reported_exceptions: Final chapter/ending should resolve rather than cliff-hang. Standalone educational content may not need hooks.
direct_evidence: S02 explicitly recommends chapter endings with forward momentum; mapping to retention/YouTube viewing is not demonstrated.
notes: S02 explicitly recommends chapter endings with forward momentum; mapping to retention/YouTube viewing is not demonstrated.

title: Pacing diagnostics — outcome patterns, sequel counts, length outliers
source_claim: Use systematic pacing checks: runs of easy wins (too many "yes" outcomes), long stretches without a sequel, length outliers (chapters too short or long), repeated resolution endings, and missing hooks.
reported_confidence: Moderate. Author-defined diagnostics, not empirically validated thresholds.
reported_exceptions: These are prompts to reread, not hard rules (stated explicitly in S01).
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Gather-point convergence as pacing tool
source_claim: In branching or complex narratives, convergence points (where multiple threads or paths rejoin) function as natural pacing beats — moments of resolution before the next divergence.
reported_scope: CD (context-dependent — most relevant to branching/complex narratives)
reported_confidence: Low-moderate. Single interactive-narrative source. Transferability to linear scripts uncertain.
reported_exceptions: Linear single-thread narratives don't have convergence points.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Dialogue does double duty — advance plot while revealing character
source_claim: Good dialogue does at least two jobs simultaneously: advancing the plot, revealing character, establishing relationships, or conveying information. Purely transactional dialogue (exposition delivery) reads as flat.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Core craft principle with cross-source support.
reported_exceptions: Some expository dialogue in educational content is necessarily transactional.
direct_evidence: S01 explicitly says dialogue/action beats can serve multiple jobs; chiefly fiction-character contexts.
notes: S01 explicitly says dialogue/action beats can serve multiple jobs; chiefly fiction-character contexts.

title: Subtext — characters deflect, understate, answer different questions
source_claim: Characters should often not say exactly what they mean. Subtext emerges through deflection, understatement, avoidance, and answering a different question than the one asked.
reported_scope: FS (fiction, dramatic nonfiction with reconstructed dialogue)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Consistent craft principle. Application to scripted narration limited.
reported_exceptions: Documentary interviews capture real speech. Educational content needs directness. Nonfiction must not fabricate dialogue (S24).
direct_evidence: S01 defines subtext through said-want vs hidden-want, not obligatory for all functional dialogue.
notes: S01 defines subtext through said-want vs hidden-want, not obligatory for all functional dialogue.

title: Characters identifiable without dialogue tags
source_claim: Each character should have distinct enough vocabulary, sentence structure, speech patterns, and preferred topics that they can be identified without attribution tags.
reported_evidence: CS (two sources with tooling support in S01)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Craft principle with tool-supported verification.
reported_exceptions: Narrator-only formats (voiceover) have a single voice. Real interview subjects have their own voices.
direct_evidence: S01 discusses differentiation of character voices; tag-free identification is an author diagnostic rather than universal objective test.
notes: S01 discusses differentiation of character voices; tag-free identification is an author diagnostic rather than universal objective test.

title: Style sheet for voice consistency across sessions
source_claim: Record dialect, spelling, capitalization, hyphenation, numbers, dialogue punctuation, and character-specific voice summaries in a style sheet. Use it to maintain consistency across writing sessions and agents.
reported_scope: U (any multi-session or multi-author content production)
reported_confidence: High. Standard editorial practice across publishing industries.
reported_exceptions: One-off short content may not need a formal style sheet.
direct_evidence: S01 prescribes a concrete book style-sheet artifact for dialect, continuity, voice differentiation.
notes: S01 prescribes a concrete book style-sheet artifact for dialect, continuity, voice differentiation.

title: Five reader reward channels as diagnostic framework
source_claim: Readers/viewers derive engagement from five overlapping channels: (1) Transportation — immersion and consistent POV, (2) Aesthetic — sentence/visual-level pleasure, (3) Social simulation — characters as minds to model, (4) Flow — pacing and comprehension ease, (5) Curiosity/prediction — information gaps, setup/payoff, suspense. Damaging one tends to damage the others.
reported_evidence: TF (theoretical framework citing research backing in resources/citations.md)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Framework cites research backing but the specific synthesis is author-constructed. Not independently validated.
reported_exceptions: Different formats weight channels differently. Educational content may emphasize flow and curiosity over social simulation.
direct_evidence: S02 reader-sim distinguishes five channels (transportation, aesthetic, social simulation, curiosity/prediction, flow). Framework is author diagnostic, not validated as exhaustive.
notes: S02 reader-sim distinguishes five channels (transportation, aesthetic, social simulation, curiosity/prediction, flow). Framework is author diagnostic, not validated as exhaustive.

title: Setup-payoff tracking with status lifecycle
source_claim: Every narrative setup (clue, promise, open question, foreshadowing, motif) should be tracked from planned → planted → paid off. Setups without payoffs are errors; payoffs without setups are cheating.
reported_evidence: CS (multiple applications within one comprehensive skill system)
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Core storytelling principle. The tracking methodology is author-specific but the principle is widely accepted.
reported_exceptions: Open-ended or literary fiction may deliberately leave questions unresolved. Real-life nonfiction may have genuinely unresolved elements.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Delayed significance — reader sees the clue before understanding it
source_claim: Information can be planted that the audience sees but doesn't understand until later, when context reveals its significance. This is fair play and enhances the sense of a cohesive narrative.
reported_scope: U (mystery, thriller, documentary revelation, nonfiction investigation)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Well-established in mystery craft. Broader application less documented.
reported_exceptions: Educational content needs immediate comprehension, not delayed significance.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Horror — three fear modes ordered deliberately: dread → terror → gross-out
source_claim: Horror works through structure, not imagery. Three modes must be sequenced: Dread (anticipation, most sustainable), Terror (confrontation, brief and costly), Gross-out (visceral disgust, cheapest, tires fastest). Build on dread, spend terror rarely, use gross-out only after dread has done its work.
reported_evidence: AR (author recommendation, consistent with King's categorization)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source, but consistent with established horror craft tradition (King, Tremblay).
reported_exceptions: Splatter/gore deliberately inverts this hierarchy. Comedy-horror mixes modes differently.
direct_evidence: S01 horror reference explicitly distinguishes dread, terror and gross-out and recommends an ordering within horror craft.
notes: S01 horror reference explicitly distinguishes dread, terror and gross-out and recommends an ordering within horror craft.

title: The uncanny — one wrong detail in something familiar
source_claim: Take something ordinary and add exactly one wrong detail. The reader's familiarity supplies the fear. Two or more wrongnesses turn into surrealism (a different effect).
reported_confidence: Low-moderate. Single source. The principle is well-known from Freud/Jentsch but the "exactly one" rule is the author's formalization.
direct_evidence: S01 horror reference explicitly defines the uncanny as familiar made wrong. Horror-only author guidance.
notes: S01 horror reference explicitly defines the uncanny as familiar made wrong. Horror-only author guidance.

title: Recovery periods after intensity peaks
source_claim: After a terror/intensity beat, give the audience a genuinely quieter scene. False safety is acceptable only if the recovery is genuinely safer, so its violation lands. Never place two terror beats back-to-back.
reported_scope: U (any content with intensity variation — horror, thriller, documentary, sports)
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Multiple sources within the same ecosystem plus independent S02 support.
direct_evidence: S01 horror reference recommends recovery after terror and warns against continuously spending tension. No causal retention study.
notes: S01 horror reference recommends recovery after terror and warns against continuously spending tension. No causal retention study.

title: One idea per sentence
source_claim: Long, complicated sentences often show the writer hasn't decided what to say. Short sentences split complex information into manageable units. Each sentence should carry one main idea.
reported_evidence: CS (two official style guides — US government + Microsoft)
reported_scope: U (universal, especially for spoken narration where re-reading isn't possible)
reported_confidence: High. Two institutional sources. Applicable to all narration formats. Consistent with plain language movement.
reported_exceptions: Literary fiction deliberately uses complex sentences. Spoken delivery may use fragments shorter than sentences.
direct_evidence: GSA recommends one idea per sentence for public information. Universal coverage of literary/audio narration not established.
notes: GSA recommends one idea per sentence for public information. Universal coverage of literary/audio narration not established.

title: Three types of transitions — pointing words, echo links, explicit connectives
source_claim: Transitions connect ideas using: (1) Pointing words (this, that, these — referencing back), (2) Echo links (repeating a concept from the previous passage), (3) Explicit connectives (however, therefore, also — stating the relationship).
reported_evidence: PP (professional practice, citing published legal writing authority)
reported_confidence: High. Established writing principle with authoritative source citation.
reported_exceptions: Rapid-fire editing in short-form video may replace verbal transitions with visual ones.
direct_evidence: S33 describes Garner three transition categories: pointing words, echo links, explicit connectives; secondhand Garner classification.
notes: S33 describes Garner three transition categories: pointing words, echo links, explicit connectives; secondhand Garner classification.

title: Avoid idioms, culture-specific references, and modifier stacks for international audiences
source_claim: International content should avoid idioms, colloquial expressions, culture-specific references, and chains of stacked modifiers. Readers in other locales may not share your country's history or culture.
reported_scope: U (any content intended for multilingual or international audiences)
reported_confidence: High. Two institutional sources with professional practice backing.
reported_exceptions: Deliberately localized content for a specific culture may use culture-specific references intentionally.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Cognitive load — teach one chunk at a time, worked examples before practice
source_claim: Working memory handles about four elements. Teach one small chunk at a time. Provide a worked example before independent practice. Fill prerequisite gaps before the main idea.
reported_evidence: TF (established educational psychology framework with stated caveats)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Well-established in classroom contexts. Extension to AI-generated and video content is explicitly flagged as unvalidated (S45 caveats.md).
reported_exceptions: Expert audiences need less scaffolding (expertise reversal effect — S45 caveats.md). Entertainment content doesn't follow pedagogical sequencing.
direct_evidence: S45 documents novice worked examples and completion tasks; broad one-chunk script recommendation is inferred.
notes: S45 documents novice worked examples and completion tasks; broad one-chunk script recommendation is inferred.

title: Voice as constant, tone as variable
source_claim: An organization's/creator's voice (personality, values) stays constant across all content. Tone (emotional register) shifts with the situation: somber for tragedy, enthusiastic for celebration, direct for technical content.
reported_confidence: High. Two institutional sources. Well-established in communications practice.
reported_exceptions: Fictional narrators may shift voice deliberately for effect.
direct_evidence: 18F directly distinguishes stable voice/personality from tone variation in its own style guide.
notes: 18F directly distinguishes stable voice/personality from tone variation in its own style guide.

title: Never present unverified knowledge as verified
source_claim: Unsourced recall stays open/unverified status. Set verified status only when every fact has a source. When sources conflict, record both sides as disputed.
reported_confidence: High. Three independent sources with strong consensus. Core journalism and research practice.
reported_exceptions: None. This is a universal epistemic principle.
direct_evidence: S01 explicitly says not to present unverified knowledge as verified. Applies to factual assertions.
notes: S01 explicitly says not to present unverified knowledge as verified. Applies to factual assertions.

title: Six-level evidence taxonomy for nonfiction
source_claim: Every key fact and scene element should be labeled by evidence strength: (1) Author witnessed, (2) Subject recollection, (3) Third-party testimony, (4) Documents, (5) Inference, (6) Unknown. Dispute points require independent corroboration.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Single primary source, but derived from established nonfiction methodology.
reported_exceptions: Fiction is exempt. Educational content uses citations differently.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Four-class source probative taxonomy
source_claim: Sources are classified as: primary proof (direct evidence), secondary proof (derivative evidence), non-probative (irrelevant to the claim), or undetermined. Classification determines evidentiary weight.
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source, but methodology traces to established historical research practice.
reported_exceptions: Entertainment and fiction don't need source classification.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Data bulletproofing — verify record counts, check for impossible values, spot-check against raw data
source_claim: Before publishing data-dependent claims: verify record counts match expectations, check for impossible/implausible values, cross-check computed results against raw data, and have someone who wasn't involved in the analysis challenge the work.
reported_scope: U (any content using data or statistics)
reported_confidence: High. Named professional author (Jennifer LaFleur), institutional backing (ProPublica), independently adapted by S27.
reported_exceptions: None for data-dependent content.
direct_evidence: ProPublica guide checks record counts, totals, ranges, missing data and source provenance.
notes: ProPublica guide checks record counts, totals, ranges, missing data and source provenance.

title: Adversarial review — the Dissertation/Opponent model
source_claim: Designate a person uninvolved in the research to formally challenge the work: question definitions, verify data usage, challenge calculations, assess conclusions, and spot-check. This formal adversarial role catches errors that self-review misses.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Two independent sources with complementary models. S09 implements with six specialized reviewer agents.
reported_exceptions: Quick-turnaround content may not allow full adversarial review.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Risk flagging — certain topics require human expert review
source_claim: Content involving legal, medical, weapons, safety, cultural, defamation, or technical claims requires review by a qualified human specialist before publication. AI research can flag and gather but never replace expert review.
reported_confidence: High. Three sources with strong consensus.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Five-level review hierarchy
source_claim: Reviews progress from big-picture to fine-detail: (1) Editorial review (what revision does this need?), (2) Developmental edit (right shape?), (3) Line edit (moves well?), (4) Copyedit (correct?), (5) Proofreading (what slipped through?). Each level assumes levels above are stable.
reported_confidence: High. Industry-standard editorial practice.
reported_exceptions: Short-form content may collapse levels. Real-time production may not allow sequential passes.
direct_evidence: S02 story-review describes developmental, line, copyedit and proofing, plus editorial review, but named hierarchy is an author process not universal law.
notes: S02 story-review describes developmental, line, copyedit and proofing, plus editorial review, but named hierarchy is an author process not universal law.

title: Nonfiction review — authenticity audit for every key claim
source_claim: For nonfiction, audit how the author knows each key fact, quote, sequence, inner state, or reconstructed scene. Label each as: firsthand, attributed, documented, corroborated, inferred, or unknown.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Single source, but methodology is well-grounded in journalism practice.
direct_evidence: S24 nonfiction review explicitly audits factual claims, quotes, actions and reconstruction provenance.
notes: S24 nonfiction review explicitly audits factual claims, quotes, actions and reconstruction provenance.

title: 26 AI writing anti-patterns
source_claim: AI-generated text exhibits recognizable patterns organized into six families: (1) Staging instead of stating, (2) Rhythm by rule, (3) Inflation and borrowed authority, (4) Formatting by rule, (5) Leftovers (chatbot residue), (6) Wrong reader. Each family contains specific detectable patterns.
reported_evidence: AR (practitioner compilation from wiki community source)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Community-sourced pattern identification. Individual pattern strength varies.
direct_evidence: S14 lists 26 cataloged patterns, explicitly traced to Wikipedia/community editing; not an exhaustive or experimentally valid AI-authorship detector.
notes: S14 lists 26 cataloged patterns, explicitly traced to Wikipedia/community editing; not an exhaustive or experimentally valid AI-authorship detector.

title: Nine-stage editorial workflow with approval gates
source_claim: Professional content production follows: intake → research → outline → draft → internal review → revision → external review → final edit → publication. Each stage has defined entry/exit criteria and status tracking.
reported_scope: U (any content production with quality requirements)
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Professional practice with detailed implementation.
reported_exceptions: Solo creators may compress stages. Breaking news may skip some gates.
direct_evidence: S09 original SKILL.md has numbered stages 1–9 (intake through performance planning). Editorial/article context.
notes: S09 original SKILL.md has numbered stages 1–9 (intake through performance planning). Editorial/article context.

title: Meaning-based translation — understand intent, find equivalent expression
source_claim: Translation should preserve meaning and intent, not literal words. Find equivalent expressions in the target language/culture. Never add or subtract meaning. Test with three questions: what does the original say, what does the target say, do they match?
reported_confidence: High. Institutional source (Mozilla) with established professional practice.
direct_evidence: S56 general localization guide directly prescribes meaning-based translation within software localization.
notes: S56 general localization guide directly prescribes meaning-based translation within software localization.

title: Culture-specific reference adaptation
source_claim: When content references culture-specific elements (metaphors, humor, references), find equivalent expressions in the target culture rather than translating literally. This is not free substitution — the equivalent must carry the same function.
reported_confidence: High. Two institutional sources.
direct_evidence: S56 supports adapting cultural idioms/references in localization; spoken storytelling transfer untested.
notes: S56 supports adapting cultural idioms/references in localization; spoken storytelling transfer untested.

title: German-specific: formal register, resist English borrowing
source_claim: German content should use formal register (never "du" except social media), prefer infinitive over imperative, and use German equivalents for English technical terms (Symbole not Icons, Schaltflaechen not Buttons).
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single institutional source for German-specific rules.
direct_evidence: S56 German style guide says avoid both informal du and, generally, Sie except direct address; ledger overstates universal formal-register rule. Also German software-brand context does not govern all German narration.
notes: S56 German style guide says avoid both informal du and, generally, Sie except direct address; ledger overstates universal formal-register rule. Also German software-brand context does not govern all German narration.

title: No fabricated dialogue, composite characters, or misleading compression
source_claim: Nonfiction must not: combine multiple people into one "real" character, invent dialogue not spoken, or apply time compression that misleads about sequence of events. A recorded departure is a choice, not an error — but it must be recorded.
reported_confidence: High. Core journalism/nonfiction ethics with institutional backing.
direct_evidence: S24 nonfiction review requires provenance for quotes/actions/reconstructions; source does not ban all compressed storytelling under every circumstance.
notes: S24 nonfiction review requires provenance for quotes/actions/reconstructions; source does not ban all compressed storytelling under every circumstance.

title: Four-stage reporting funnel with stop conditions
source_claim: Nonfiction research progresses: (1) Broad exploration with upper time limits, (2) Narrow to key people/scenes/documents, (3) Set stop conditions (what evidence is "enough" for a structural sketch), (4) Use the sketch to expose remaining gaps.
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Single source with strong methodological grounding.
direct_evidence: S24 source map identifies four-stage reporting funnel as synthesis of curriculum chapters; not an original tested framework.
notes: S24 source map identifies four-stage reporting funnel as synthesis of curriculum chapters; not an original tested framework.

title: Subject rights — consent, privacy, power imbalance, harm assessment
source_claim: Before publication, assess: informed consent (signing authorization ≠ sufficient understanding of consequences), identity protection needs, power dynamics between reporter and subject, potential real-world harm from publication, and reporter involvement effects.
reported_confidence: High. Ethical principles with strong professional backing.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Mystery — fair-play doctrine
source_claim: The reader must receive every clue the detective uses, early enough to solve the case. The culprit appears in the first third. The detective knows nothing the reader doesn't. The solution must be the best explanation of planted clues.
reported_evidence: TF (established genre convention — Van Dine/Knox tradition)
reported_confidence: High within genre. Established convention, not empirically tested but genre-defining.
direct_evidence: S01 mystery reference explicitly states fair-play clue access principles; genre conventions, not universal scriptwriting law.
notes: S01 mystery reference explicitly states fair-play clue access principles; genre conventions, not universal scriptwriting law.

title: Mystery — clue planting techniques
source_claim: Four techniques: (1) Hidden in plain sight (clue as set dressing), (2) Camouflaged (one false element among true ones), (3) Misinterpreted (correctly observed, wrongly explained), (4) Absence as clue (something expected is missing).
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source. Techniques are individually well-known.
direct_evidence: S01 describes planted, camouflaged, misinterpreted, absence clues; only for mystery craft.
notes: S01 describes planted, camouflaged, misinterpreted, absence clues; only for mystery craft.

title: Horror — monster rules must be established before exploitation
source_claim: Whatever the threat is, its rules (capabilities, limitations, protections against it) must be set before they're used in the plot. Characters must make informed bad decisions, not arbitrary ones. Rules must stay consistent.
reported_evidence: AR (author recommendation, consistent with horror craft tradition)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source but consistent with genre expectations.
direct_evidence: S01 horror reference asks for consistent monster rules and their disclosure before exploitation, a genre-specific practice.
notes: S01 horror reference asks for consistent monster rules and their disclosure before exploitation, a genre-specific practice.

title: Interactive narrative — text-first authoring
source_claim: In interactive narrative systems, dialogue/text is the default layer, with mechanics (choices, variables, flow control) layered on top. The writing itself should read naturally without the mechanics being visible.
reported_confidence: Moderate. Two sources. Transferability to linear scripts is assessed as partially applicable.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Three-dimensional prose rating — novelty, clarity, prose quality
source_claim: Written content can be rated on three independent scales: Novelty (A-F: novel ideas through derivative), Clarity (A-F: crystal through chaotic), Prose quality (A-F: inspired through weak). Overall rating equals the lowest individual rating.
reported_confidence: Low-moderate. Single source. Useful heuristic, not validated against human judgment.
reported_exceptions: Creative fiction may deliberately sacrifice clarity for artistic effect.
notes: Direct source content not checked in this batch; ledger claim is not approved.

title: Atomic fact decomposition for factual verification
source_claim: Text can be decomposed into "atomic facts" — smallest standalone units of information that can be independently verified. Each atomic fact is then checked against knowledge sources to compute an accuracy score (FActScore).
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Academic research with published methodology. Measures factual precision, not narrative quality.
reported_exceptions: Fiction and opinion content don't have verifiable atomic facts. Subjective claims resist decomposition.
direct_evidence: FActScore performs atomic factual decomposition of long-form generated factual biographies; transfer to creative fiction is unsupported.
notes: FActScore performs atomic factual decomposition of long-form generated factual biographies; transfer to creative fiction is unsupported.

title: LLM writing anti-patterns — measurable dimensions
source_claim: LLM-generated prose exhibits measurable differences from human writing: lower burstiness (less sentence-length variation), narrower character name pools ("Elara Phenomenon"), higher semantic similarity between passages, lower n-gram diversity, and persistent phonetic patterns even when surface variation is introduced.
reported_scope: U (detecting and avoiding AI writing patterns)
reported_confidence: Moderate. Single source with quantitative analysis. Generalizability requires replication.

title: 15-question story evaluation rubric

title: Psychic distance — control narrative proximity for emotional effect
source_claim: Narration exists on a continuum from far ("It was winter of the year 1853") to close ("Snow. Under your collar, freezing and plugging up your miserable soul."). Move closer for emotional peaks and character-defining moments; pull back for transitions and establishing context. The rhythm of close and far gives prose its emotional shape.

title: Free indirect discourse — narrator's voice colored by character's perspective
source_claim: Blend the narrator's voice with the character's perspective so third-person narration carries the character's vocabulary, judgment, and worldview. Conventional: "Connie thought she was pretty and believed that was the most important thing." Free indirect: "She knew she was pretty and that was everything."

title: Sensory grounding — character-filtered specificity over catalog
source_claim: "The forest" is nowhere. "Pine needles crunching underfoot, the smell of wet bark" is a place. Use one or two vivid, specific details rather than cataloging all five senses. What a character notices reveals who they are — sensory detail should be filtered through POV.

title: Show-through-action calibration — tell for logistics, show for what matters
source_claim: Show character states through behavior, dialogue, and physical response — but apply this selectively. Tell for logistics ("Three weeks passed"). Show for moments that matter. Showing everything is as exhausting as telling everything. The anti-pattern is not telling itself, but labeling emotions: "She felt sad" (label) vs. "She kept reaching for her phone to text him before remembering" (interiority showing grief).

reported_exceptions: Expository content may appropriately label states directly.

title: Sentence rhythm — vary length and structure with intention
source_claim: Short sentences create tension, shock, emphasis. Longer cumulative sentences create immersion, reflection, complex emotion. Fragments suggest intimacy, interrupted thought. When every sentence follows the same pattern (subject-verb-object-repeat), prose flattens regardless of content. LLMs exhibit measurably lower burstiness (less sentence-length variation) than human writers.

reported_confidence: High. Three sources including empirical measurement.

title: Nine structural LLM failure modes traced to training incentives
source_claim: LLM-generated prose exhibits nine structural failure modes, each traceable to the training reward for complete, thorough, resolved, clear responses: (1) Over-elaborating scope — writing aftermath + reflection + teaser beyond the brief, (2) Flattening voice — same competent-but-even register throughout, (3) Info-dumping — narration pauses to explain how things work, (4) Labeling emotions — "She was furious" instead of showing, (5) Resolving tension prematurely — every conflict gets same-scene resolution, (6) Homogenizing characters — everyone sounds articulate and insightful, (7) Adding emotional commentary — metaphor explaining what just happened, (8) Collapsing ambiguity — tipping moral situations toward one answer, (9) Over-intensifying language — "profound emptiness" where "I miss you" lands harder.

reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Single comprehensive source. Root-cause analysis adds explanatory depth.

title: Three empirically documented LLM prose failure modes
source_claim: Three LLM writing failures have empirical documentation: (1) Syntactic templating — repeated sentence structures even when content changes (Shaib et al. 2024, EMNLP), (2) Stock physical tells — rubber-stamp body signifiers (clenched fists, shaky breaths) applied mechanically to satisfy show-don't-tell (fix: character-specific behavior, not different body parts), (3) Attractor-state fluency — prose feels "smoothed" rather than "written," every passage has same measured control regardless of scene stakes (arxiv 2406.05587, "Creativity Has Left the Chat," 2024).

title: Evidence hierarchy for AI writing antipatterns
source_claim: AI writing tells should be classified by evidence quality: (1) Research-backed — measurably different from human writing via validated instruments (lower lexical variability, fewer personal pronouns, positive-emotion skew, shallow interiority, low dialogue subtext), (2) Community-identified — consistently observed but not formally measured (clean-but-hollow prose, generic arc progression, repetitive emotional choreography, tidy-summary endings), (3) Explicitly unreliable — word-level "slop lists" (delve, tapestry, etc.) are model-version-dependent, prompt-dependent, and genre-confounded.

title: Modality effect — narrate visuals, don't caption them
source_claim: When two visual sources must be integrated, present one in audio (narration) instead of on-screen text. Animation + narration > animation + on-screen text. This is the fundamental cognitive justification for voiceover-based educational video. Based on Baddeley's working memory model (partially independent visual-spatial and phonological subsystems).
reported_scope: FS (educational/explainer video with high element-interactivity content)

reported_exceptions: For low-complexity material, the modality effect is useless — there is no overload to relieve. Accessibility requirements may demand on-screen text (captions, hearing-impaired viewers).

title: Split-attention effect — integrate related information spatially and temporally
source_claim: When two information sources must be mentally integrated, place them together rather than separating them. In video: place labels directly on diagrams. Do not say "as you can see in the diagram on the right" while showing text on the left. Narration should describe what is visually present.
reported_confidence: High. Peer-reviewed CLT finding corroborated by independent production practice.

title: Redundancy effect — don't narrate on-screen text
source_claim: When one information source is self-sufficient, the second source adds load rather than helping — learners cannot easily ignore redundant material. In video: do not read on-screen text aloud. If a diagram is self-explanatory, do not also describe it in words. Conflict with accessibility resolved per-project.

title: Expertise reversal — designs that help novices hurt experts
source_claim: Most instructional design effects invert as learner expertise grows. Worked examples help novices but bore experts. Integrated text+diagram helps novices but creates redundancy for experts. Audio+visual helps novices but overloads experts on familiar material. A single script going to all expertise levels simultaneously cannot optimize for all — explicit "skip ahead if you know X" callouts or separate beginner/advanced versions are workarounds.
reported_scope: U (meta-principle: any instructional or explanatory content)
reported_confidence: High. Convergent finding across pedagogical research and AI-writing practice.

title: Scaffolding fading across a series — worked examples → completion problems → independent practice
source_claim: In a series or course, reduce scaffolding over time. Early episodes: full worked examples. Middle episodes: partial examples (learner completes remaining steps). Later episodes: present the problem and let the viewer attempt it. This prevents the expertise reversal effect from degrading later content.
reported_confidence: High. Multiple peer-reviewed CLT effects combined.

title: All readability formulas were normed on written text reading — none validated for listening
source_claim: Every standard readability formula (Flesch, SMOG, Gunning Fog, Flesch-Kincaid, ARI, Coleman-Liau, Dale-Chall) was developed for and validated against written prose comprehension. title: No existing text metrics measure the dimensions most critical for script quality
source_claim: Existing text quality tools measure readability, coherence, and lexical diversity — but none measure narrative arc, emotional engagement, spoken rhythm, hook effectiveness, pacing appropriate to delivery speed, call-to-action clarity, or conversational naturalness. These unmeasured dimensions are the ones that matter most for script quality. The most applicable existing metric is TextDescriptives' sentence-to-sentence semantic coherence (originally developed for analyzing spoken language in clinical settings), which captures real semantic flow without requiring a reference text.

source_claim: Plot is driven by revelations — surprising information that forces characters (and the audience) to re-evaluate what they know. Revelations must be logical (based on planted information), build in intensity, and arrive at increasing pace. A well-structured story contains 7–10 major reveals minimum. The audience revelation (audience learns what the hero does not) is a distinct and powerful beat.

title: Forge Point convergence crises — all narrative strands in simultaneous crisis
source_claim: At key structural turning points (Forge Points), ALL narrative strands must be in simultaneous crisis. The protagonist cannot resolve all crises and must choose what to sacrifice. Sacrifices escalate across the story: safety → innocence → trust → a life → essential identity. This is the structural mechanism that creates meaningful choices and prevents arbitrary plot turns.

title: Mercy Engine — victory through consequences of mercy, not power
source_claim: In long-form fiction, victory should flow through the consequences of earlier mercy, not through superior force. Structure 4+ acts of mercy with escalating costs throughout the story. Each mercy must cost something real; the recipient must be credibly dangerous; the payoff must be unexpected by the protagonist. The structural function is to prevent "might makes right," reward character over capability, and differentiate protagonist from antagonist.

title: Dark Mirror antagonist — parallel origin, comprehensible divergence, kernel of truth
source_claim: The most effective antagonist shares the protagonist's origin (mentor, power source, trauma, or goal) with a comprehensible divergence point. The antagonist's philosophy must contain a genuine kernel of truth — they must be dangerously, partially right. Victory methods: mercy returning, philosophy turned against them, redemption sparked, argument answered through action, or the cost coming due. Victory through superior force is explicitly rejected.

title: Motivation coherence — characters act for internal reasons, not plot convenience
source_claim: Characters must act for reasons consistent with their history, values, emotional state, and current knowledge. The most common failure: characters doing what the plot requires without sufficient internal justification. Major shifts need precipitating events — the solution is not adding an explanatory paragraph but making the character's situation lead naturally to the action. Regression is valid (characters don't progress linearly). Flat arcs are valid (not every character needs to change). The variation in articulation, insight, and emotional fluency IS the characterization — homogenizing these is an LLM failure mode.
reported_evidence: PP (professional practice within comprehensive craft system)
reported_confidence: Moderate-high. Single source ecosystem but addresses known LLM failure mode with specific countermeasures.

title: Four-corner opposition — characters as different approaches to the central moral problem
source_claim: Place the hero, main opponent, and two other characters at corners of a value square, each representing a different approach to the story's central moral problem. This creates a web of conflict rather than a single line of opposition. The opponent must want the same goal or a competing one, and must attack the hero's great weakness. At self-revelation, both hero and opponent should undergo change (double reversal).
